title: Body and the Senses in Spatial Experience: The Implications of Kinesthetic and Synesthetic Perceptions for Design Thinking
central_proposition: Consideration of the kinesthetic and synesthetic body, rooted in embodied and multisensory experience, can deepen and challenge existing visual-centric models of spatial perception in design thinking, leading to more holistic and empathetic design outcomes.

concept_definitions.name: design thinking
concept_definitions.definition: A process that often disconnects conceptual thinking from physical expression or process, emphasizing visuality and sometimes overlooking the body's role.

concept_definitions.name: spatial perception
concept_definitions.definition: Multimodal and fundamentally bound to the body, involving tangible elements, intangible attributes (atmosphere, energy), and cognitive processing of sensory input.

concept_definitions.name: embodiment
concept_definitions.definition: The tangible or visible form of perceived concept and meaning through which ordinary life is incorporated into the body and becomes naturalized in the form of space.

concept_definitions.name: lived body
concept_definitions.definition: Comprised of continuous felt experiences, representing a 'self of movement' or 'feeling of doing' that ties felt, experienced, and sensed body together.

concept_definitions.name: kinesthetic perception
concept_definitions.definition: Humans' ability to sense muscular movement from the lived body, a direct sensitivity to movement through internally mediated neuro-muscular systems, enabling awareness of body location and position in relation to surroundings.

concept_definitions.name: synesthetic perception
concept_definitions.definition: A physio-psychological and cross-modal sensory phenomenon where a stimulus in one sense modality immediately evokes sensations in one or more different sense modalities, autonomous, involuntary, and irrepressible.

concept_definitions.name: sensorium commune
concept_definitions.definition: Merleau-Ponty's concept of a human whose body accesses the world through the senses, where perception is a 'flow of experiences' rather than a mere collection of object perceptions.

argument_structure: The argument begins by critiquing the visual-centric bias and analytical fragmentation of senses in traditional design thinking and perception models. It then introduces phenomenological perspectives on the lived body, action-perception coupling, and multisensory experience. Building on these foundations, it defines and elaborates on kinesthetic and synesthetic perceptions, providing architectural examples. Finally, it proposes three novel design thinking models (Synesthetic Translation, Kinesthetic Resonance, and Kinesthetic Engagement) that integrate these concepts to foster more embodied and empathetic design processes.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core mechanism is that the body is not a passive receptor but an active agent whose movements, internal states (interoception, proprioception), and multisensory integration (synesthesia) actively construct spatial meaning and experience. This embodied, action-based perception allows for a holistic understanding of space that transcends individual sensory modalities. By integrating these 'felt' and 'cross-sensory' experiences into design thinking, designers can move beyond abstract visual representations to create environments that resonate more deeply with human lived experience, fostering empathy and richer spatial configurations.

findings.antecedent: Design disciplines' emphasis on visuality above other sensory domains
findings.consequent: Weaknesses undermining certain aspects of spatial experience
findings.mechanism: Restricting perception to a particular modality fails to fully explain diverse sensory phenomena in multidimensional space.
findings.quote: design disciplines have emphasized the visuality above the other sensory domains

findings.antecedent: Approaches to human perception treating senses as independent
findings.consequent: Incomplete understanding of multimodal spatial experience
findings.mechanism: Senses are distinct yet indiscernible, united through the body in becoming its perception (Merleau-Ponty).
findings.quote: approaches to human perception sometimes seem overly analytical, the consequence of which is that the senses are often treated as if they worked independently
findings.empirical_support_cited: Pallasmaa, 2005; Dischinger, 2006; Franck and Lepori, 2007; Heylighen et al., 2009; Heylighen, 2011; Wastiels et al., 2013; Kwon and Kim, 2021

findings.consequent: Interdependence on the physical structure of the body
findings.mechanism: The body is not separate from the mind, and mobility is the primary vector and provider of meaning in represented space.
findings.quote: the way the human being perceives space is interdependent on the physical structure of the body.

findings.mechanism: The body acts as an active agent, mediating the relationship between mind, body, idea, and space.
findings.quote: The body apprehends the experience in which one's kinesthetic engagement and knowledge play an essential role.

findings.antecedent: Consideration of body movement as a sensory modality and ground for spatial experience
findings.consequent: Lack of discussion in relation to creativity and design thinking
findings.mechanism: Despite accepted perspective that design mediates movement, body movement has been overlooked as a sensory modality.
findings.quote: there has been a lack of consideration of body movement as a sensory modality and the ground for the possibility of spatial experience

findings.consequent: Mind (brain)-body connection in perception and cognition
findings.mechanism: Embodiment refers to the tangible form of perceived concept and meaning, integrating ordinary life into the body and space.
findings.quote: embracing the phenomenological concept of embodiment

findings.antecedent: Kinesthetic sense (direct sensitivity to movement through internally mediated neuro-muscular systems)
findings.consequent: Ability to gain awareness of body's location and position in relation to surroundings
findings.mechanism: Kinesthesia is a physical, holistic form of recognition that aids in intuitive and instinctual recognition of physical location characteristics.
findings.quote: Humans possess a kinesthetic sense, affording them the ability to gain awareness of their body's location and position in relation to their surroundings.

findings.antecedent: Kinesthetic experience (involving body schema, exteroception, interoception, proprioception)
findings.mechanism: It is a high level of perception that involves complex constitution of body schema and representation of body's spatial properties.
findings.quote: It is a high level of perception that involves the complex constitution of body schema, the representation of the body's spatial properties, including exteroception, interoception, and proprioception

findings.mechanism: Kinesthetic experience is contextual and relational, where tactile phenomena disappear if spatiality or temporality is removed.
findings.quote: the spatiotemporality of the lived body actualizes the articulation of sensory phenomena

findings.consequent: New mode of creative thinking and diverse perspectives on sensory phenomena and spatial experiences for designers
findings.mechanism: Understanding the cross-modality of the senses helps designers establish new ways of conceptualizing and interpreting spatial experiences.
findings.quote: understanding the cross-modality of the senses may help designers establish a new mode of creative thinking and diverse perspectives on sensory phenomena and spatial experiences.

findings.antecedent: Synesthetic Translation Model (participant's narrative of auditory experience + designers' synesthetic interpretation + self-experience/reflection)
findings.mechanism: This model involves a conceptual translation process, converting verbal descriptions of lived, multisensory experiences (e.g., music's vibrations, volumes, cadences) into spatial attributes like compression/expansion, volume, scale, and pattern, often resulting in linear or spiral 'journeys'.
findings.quote: The Synesthetic Translation Model (Figure 5) involves a participant's (other) narrative of an auditory (e.g., musical) experience, designers' (self) synesthetic interpretation of the non-visual and intangible sensory properties and qualities the participant describes, and the designers' self-experience and reflection of the interactive context and event with the individual.

findings.antecedent: Kinesthetic Resonance Model (designers' observation of others' kinematic parameters + self-experience of event + sensory factors)
findings.mechanism: This model integrates 'vicarious engagement' with others' movements, where designers' empathy and observation of kinematic parameters (e.g., amplitude, turning velocity, balance) inform spatial design, often leading to circular, spiral, or curvilinear configurations.
findings.quote: The Kinesthetic Resonance Model (Figure 6) integrates the kinematic parameters of others (e.g., inspirational art performers, prospective occupants/users, and passers-by) observed by an audience (i.e., designers) into design thinking.

findings.antecedent: Kinesthetic Engagement Model (designers' bodily engagement with physical settings + peripersonal space + corporeal & kinetic experience + sensory factors)
findings.mechanism: This model emphasizes an 'embodied design process' where designers use their own body movements, postures, and interactions with the physical setting to determine forms and scale, resulting in non-linear, multiaxial spatial configurations.
findings.quote: The Kinesthetic Engagement Model (Figure 7) proposes that designers use their own body to determine forms and the scale in ideation.

findings.antecedent: Consideration of the kinesthetic or synesthetic body in design disciplines
findings.consequent: Deepened and challenged existing models of perceptual aspects of environmental psychology
findings.mechanism: Integrating these embodied and multisensory perspectives allows for a more comprehensive understanding of human-environment interaction beyond traditional visual-centric or analytical approaches.
findings.quote: This article suggests how consideration of the kinesthetic or synesthetic body can deepen and challenge the existing models of the perceptual aspects of environmental psychology adopted in design disciplines.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Design processes incorporating kinesthetic and synesthetic perceptions will lead to spatial configurations that are perceived as more empathetic and holistically engaging than those derived from purely visual-centric approaches.
Designers using the Synesthetic Translation Model will produce spatial designs that are described with richer multisensory and temporal narratives by occupants compared to traditional methods.

The Kinesthetic Resonance Model will result in spatial designs that evoke stronger vicarious engagement and empathy in observers, measurable through physiological or self-report metrics related to movement and emotion.

Designers employing the Kinesthetic Engagement Model will create spaces that better accommodate diverse body movements and interactions, leading to higher perceived usability and comfort for a range of users.

Empirical studies can compare occupant responses (e.g., aesthetic judgment, emotional valence, perceived restorativeness) to spaces designed using the proposed models versus conventional methods, measuring both subjective and objective indicators.
bridge_warrants: Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology provides conceptual and theoretical insights into body, senses, and perception, concretizing human existence, subjective experience, intentionality, action, and meaning.
Embodied cognition theories support the mind-body connection in perception and cognition, emphasizing sensorimotor approaches.
Multisensory integration is fundamental to spatial perception, where senses are distinct yet indiscernible and united through the body.
The neurological interpretation of haptic perception, interoception, and proprioception provides a scientific basis for action-based perception and embodied cognition.
methodological_critiques: Existing 'design thinking' models often disconnect conceptual thinking from physical expression, echoing body-mind dualism.

Design disciplines have historically emphasized visuality above other sensory domains, relying heavily on Gestalt principles which do not adequately explain corporeal and kinesthetic aspects of spatial perception.
Traditional approaches to human perception are often overly analytical, treating senses as if they worked independently.
The traditional concept of 'quale' (plural 'qualia') does not properly explain certain sensory phenomena such as synesthesia, as it restricts vision to visual quale and sound to sonorous quale.
Narrative methods, while promoting imagination, may interfere with the visual representation of designers' ideas.
model_structure:
The paper proposes three distinct design thinking models: 
1.  **Synesthetic Translation Model**: Focuses on translating a participant's multisensory narrative (e.g., auditory experience) into spatial configurations through the designer's synesthetic interpretation, emphasizing a 'journey' or linear/spiral progression.
2.  **Kinesthetic Resonance Model**: Integrates designers' observation of others' kinematic parameters (e.g., dance movements) and their own self-experience to inform spatial design, leading to configurations that resonate with movement dynamics.
3.  **Kinesthetic Engagement Model**: Emphasizes the designer's direct bodily engagement (movement, postures, interactions) with physical settings to ideate and determine spatial forms and scale, resulting in non-linear, multiaxial designs.
limitations: The proposed models were developed as pedagogical frameworks for an entry-level interior design studio course, suggesting they may require further refinement for broader application or advanced contexts.
The paper acknowledges that some sensory responses of the body (e.g., phantom sensations in VR) are seldom integrated into design thinking and remain to be explored.
crossref_title: Body and the Senses in Spatial Experience: The Implications of Kinesthetic and Synesthetic Perceptions for Design Thinking
crossref_abstract: Human perception has long been a critical subject of design thinking. While various studies have stressed the link between thinking and acting, particularly in spatial experience, the term “design thinking” seems to disconnect conceptual thinking from physical expression or process. Spatial perception is multimodal and fundamentally bound to the body that is not a mere receptor of sensory stimuli but an active agent engaged with the perceivable environment. The body apprehends the experience in which one’s kinesthetic engagement and knowledge play an essential role. Although design disciplines have integrated the abstract, metaphoric, and visual aspects of the body and its movement into conceptual thinking, studies have pointed out that design disciplines have emphasized visuality above the other sensory domains and heavily engaged with the perception of visual configurations, relying on the Gestalt principles. Gestalt psychology must be valued for its attention to a whole. However, the theories of design elements and principles over-empathizing such visuality posit the aesthetics of design mainly as visual value and understate other sensorial and perceptual aspects. Although the visual approach may provide a practical means to represent and communicate ideas, a design process heavily driven by visuality can exhibit weaknesses undermining certain aspects of spatial experience despite the complexity. Grounded in Merleau-Ponty’s notion of multisensory perception, this article discusses the relationship between body awareness and spatial perception and its implication for design disciplines concerning built environments. Special attention is given to the concepts of kinesthetic and synesthetic phenomena known as multisensory and cross-sensory, respectively. This discussion integrates the corporeal and spatiotemporal realms of human experience into the discourse of kinesthetic and synesthetic perceptions. Based on the conceptual, theoretical, and precedent analyses, this article proposes three models for design thinking: Synesthetic Translation, Kinesthetic Resonance, and Kinesthetic Engagement. To discuss the concepts rooted in action-based perception and embodied cognition, this study borrows the neurological interpretation of haptic perception, interoception, and proprioception of space. This article suggests how consideration of the kinesthetic or synesthetic body can deepen and challenge the existing models of the perceptual aspects of environmental psychology adopted in design disciplines.
